## Main result


{{< include svdmaintheorem.qmd >}}

::: {.proof}
Bla bla bla
:::




Let $A = U \Sigma V^T$ be the SVD of the $m \times n$ matrix $A$, 
and let $\mathbf{u}_{j}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ be the  $j$-th column of $U$ and $V$, respectively, i.e.,
\begin{align*}
U &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{2} & \cdots & \mathbf{u}_{m}\end{pmatrix} &
V &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}_{1} & \mathbf{v}_{2} & \cdots & \mathbf{v}_n\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*}

Clearly 
$$U \Sigma =  \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \sigma_{2}\mathbf{u}_{2}  & \cdots & \sigma_{r} \mathbf{u}_{r} & \mathbf{0} & \cdots & \mathbf{0}\end{pmatrix},$$
where the number of zero-vectors is $n-r$.
Inserting this in the outer form of matrix multiplication (@prp-matrixpodytreform) gives that
$$
\begin{aligned}
A =U \Sigma V^T= \sum_{j=1}^{p}\, (U \Sigma)_{:j} (V^T)_{j:}
= \sum_{j=1}^{r} \, \sigma_j \mathbf{u}_j ((V_{:j})^T = \sum_{j=1}^{r} \sigma_j \mathbf{u}_j \mathbf{v}_{j}^T.
\end{aligned}
$$



This shows that only the $r$ first columns of $U$ and $V$ matter in the SVD $A = U \Sigma V^T$.
Note also that all summands in $\sum_{j=1}^{r} \sigma_j \mathbf{u}_j \mathbf{v}_{j}^T$ are rank 1 matrices, since 
$$\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T = \begin{pmatrix} v_{1}\mathbf{u} & v_{2}\mathbf{u} & \cdots & v_{n}\mathbf{u}\end{pmatrix}$$
so that $\text{rank}( \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T ) = 1$ when
$\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are both nonzero. 
Thus, a matrix of rank $r$ can be written as a sum of $r$ rank one matrices.




::: {#prp-rankres}
Let $A$ have rank $r$.

* $\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots ,\mathbf{u}_r \}$ is a basis for Col$A$.
* $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots ,\mathbf{v}_r \}$ is a basis for Row$(A)$= Col$(A^T)$.

:::

::: {.proof}
Note first that for $1\leq s\leq r$ we have that
$$A\mathbf{v}_s = \sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_j \mathbf{u_j}\mathbf{v_j}^T \mathbf{v}_s = \sigma_s \mathbf{u_s},$$
since the $\mathbf{v}_s$ provide an orthonormal basis. 
It follows that all $\mathbf{u_s}$ are in the column space of $A$, so that $\text{Span}( \mathbf{u}_1,...,\mathbf{u}_k) \subseteq \text{Col}A$. 
Since column $s$ in $A$ is
$$\sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_j \mathbf{u_j}(\mathbf{v_j}^T)_s,$$
it follows that also $\text{Col}A \subseteq \text{Span}( \mathbf{u}_1,...,\mathbf{u}_r )$. 
Therefore $\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots , \mathbf{u}_r \}$ is a basis for $\text{Col}(A)$. 

For the second point, note first that $A^T = V \Sigma^T U^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A^T$.
From the above and the singular value decomposition of $A$ it follows that 
$\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}, \ldots , \mathbf{v}_r \}$ is a basis for Col $A^T$, 
and therefore also a basis for Row $A$. 
:::

## Image compression based on the singular value decomposition

In this section we will analyse what kind of information the SVD captures, 
and illustrate how it provides a method for compressing images by 
reducing storage requirements. For $1 \leq k \leq r$ we define
$$A^{(k)} = \sum_{j=1}^k \sigma_j \mathbf{u_j}\mathbf{v_j}^T.$$ {#eq-Ak}
$A^{(k)}$ has rank $k$ and can thus be thought of as a rank $k$ approximation to $A$. 
How many terms we need to include, i.e., how big $k$ must be for an acceptable approximation, 
will of course depend on the singular values, and how quickly they tend to $0$.
From @prp-rankres it follows that

* $\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots ,\mathbf{u}_k \}$ is a basis for Col$A^{(k)}$.
* $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots ,\mathbf{v}_k \}$ is a basis for Row$(A^{(k)})$.

computes the SVD of the matrix, and returns the matrix $A^{(k)}$ in @eq-Ak.

Since the rank of the image matrix equals the number of nonzero singular values, 
a low rank means that we can represent the matrix with just a few values. 
Consider the matrix below, which also is displayed as an image. 

```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
{{< include code2d.py >}}
```


The image is constant in each column. If $v_i$ is the value in column $i$, the matrix can be written as 
$\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 & v_2 & \cdots & v_n \end{pmatrix}$, which clearly is 
a rank one matrix.


Singular values are listed in decreasing order with the biggest first. 
Thus, the most ''important'' information is found in the first terms in $\sum_{j=1}^{r} \sigma_j \mathbf{u}_j \mathbf{v}_{j}^T$.

The following code plots the singular values of the matrix corresponding to the Marilyn Monroe image 
against those of a random image of the same size, and with pixel values in the same interval ($\sigma_j$ as a function of $j$).
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
{{< include code3a.py >}}
```
The singular values seem to decay much faster for the Marilyn Monroe image than for the random image. 
An informal explanation for this is that the random image has a greater degree of unorder, more *details*, 
so that one needs more singular values to describe it.



Every term in the sum in @eq-Ak needs two vectors, in addition to one singular value. 
To store the matrix $A^{(k)}$ we therefore only need to store the $k$ first vectors in both matrices $U$ and $V$, as well as the $k$
first singular values. One thus needs $k(m+n+1)$ values to store a rank $k$ SVD approximation. This can have much to say for storage:
If most of the singular values are small, we may get acceptable quality by zeroing out all singular values except the few biggest ones. 
As an example, a $500\times 500$ image has 250 000 pixel values. 
Storing the first $20$ singular components would require $20\times 1001\approx 20 000$ values, which amounts to about $8\%$ of the original storage.

As $k$ increases the rank $k$ SVD approximation gets visually closer to the original. 
For $k\approx 50$ the quality seems to be acceptable, for $k\approx 100$ it is near perfect.

The *relative error* between the matrices $A$ and $A^{(k)}$  is defined as
\begin{equation*}
  e_{rel} = \frac{\| A - A^{(k)} \|_F}{ \|A\|_F},
\end{equation*} 
where the *Frobenius norm* of an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ is defined by
$$\| B \|_F = \sqrt{ \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n  {b_{i,j}}^2 }.$$
